description:
THE FIX IS RIGHT AND ITS STATED GOAL IS NOT YET ACHIEVED.

G-26 hoisted the stage-0 auto-upgrade out of the branch-enable transaction and stopped it failing
silently: the failure is now logged at console.error and RETURNED through a well-formed discriminated
union, Stage0AutoUpgradeOutcome (product-branch-service.ts:134), whose success arm carries
`failed?: false; reason?: never` so a success-with-a-reason cannot be constructed. That part is sound.

The commit's own comment states the purpose: "it is logged at ERROR and RETURNED, so the caller and
the two UI surfaces that read stage0AutoUpgrade can say the upgrade did not happen instead of implying
it did."

THEY CANNOT. Both consumers re-declare the shape INLINE and omit the new fields:
  the-firm-practice/page.tsx:108   stage0AutoUpgrade?: { upgraded: number; blocked: number }
  PmsEnablementSection.tsx:66      stage0AutoUpgrade?: { upgraded: number; blocked: number }
Neither imports Stage0AutoUpgradeOutcome. So neither can branch on `failed`, and a customer still
cannot tell "there was nobody to upgrade" from "the upgrade failed" -- both render as
upgraded: 0, blocked: 0.

WHY TYPESCRIPT DOES NOT CATCH THIS, which is the transferable part: structural typing accepts a
NARROWER inline type against a wider return. Omitting a field is not an error; it is a legal
projection. Had either consumer imported the exported union instead of re-declaring the shape, adding
`failed` would have forced them to handle it. RE-DECLARING A RETURN TYPE INLINE OPTS OUT OF EVERY
FUTURE CHANGE TO IT, silently.

Fix is small: import Stage0AutoUpgradeOutcome in both consumers and branch on `failed` to render the
reason. Not launch-blocking -- this is strictly better than before the hoist, because the ERROR log
now exists and an operator can find it. What is missing is the customer-facing half.
justification: The remediation was designed correctly and stopped one step short of its own goal. Worth recording precisely because the code, the type and the comment are all right -- the defect lives in two consumers that opted out of the contract by restating it.
fix_files: NOT FIXED - two-line change in each consumer; surface belongs to the R80 session

description:
COMMENT ROT, CREATED BY THE FIX ITSELF, AND NOT COVERED BY THE ROT CHECK.

autoUpgradeStage0UsersOnBranchEnable carries a header describing the OLD behaviour in the PRESENT
TENSE, after f127e3c8 changed it:
  "The call there is wrapped in a try/catch that only console.warn()s"      -- it now console.error()s
                                                                              and returns a typed outcome
  "in dev/test the throw is swallowed and NO stage-0 user is ever auto-upgraded"  -- the hoist fixed this
  "threading the handle IS the whole fix"  -- this is the exact conclusion the hoist OVERTURNED;
                                              threading was rejected because ai_assistants RLS requires
                                              current_user_id() = user_id and the enclosing transaction
                                              carries the admin

A reader arriving at this function is told the pre-fix world is the current one, and is told the
remedy is the one that was tried and rejected. That is worse than no comment: it is a confident,
specific, wrong instruction sitting directly above correct code.

NOT CAUGHT BY scripts/check-comment-rot.mjs, because that check verifies a registered anchor still
EXISTS -- it cannot detect a comment that survives while the behaviour it describes changes underneath
it. That is the limit of the design and worth stating: the check catches deletion, not divergence.
This entry is the counter-example that proves it.
justification: This programme has repeatedly found that a stale explanation sends the next reader chasing the wrong thing. Here the stale text names the rejected remedy as the whole fix, so the most likely next action a reader takes is the one that would re-break it.

description:
Clicking the Permits pill offers these verbs: "Add drawing", "Upload document", "Run report",
"File minutes", "Run WPR", "New finance budget". NOT ONE CONCERNS PERMITS, and the first navigates to
/drawings/new.

The verb exists -- the dashboard's own frequent-actions row carries "Add permit" -- so this is not a
missing capability. The Permits pill's DESTINATION and its OFFERING disagree.

Same family as the Analysis pill resolving to work-progress (fixed in projexa 065fff1): a pill whose
identity is correct in one resolution path and wrong in another. Two instances now, which makes it a
pattern rather than a one-off, and suggests the verb list is resolved from something other than the
module the pill resolves to.

FOUND ONLY BECAUSE A TEST FINALLY RAN. The d603 click sweep had never completed in the spec's life --
an assertion above it failed first on every run - so nothing below it had ever executed. Reordering
that assertion is what surfaced this. Worth recording: a test that fails early hides every check
after it, and the hidden ones are invisible rather than red.

Not launch-blocking: the pill navigates somewhere real and the honest-gap path answers unexecutable
sentences. But a user clicking Permits and being offered "Add drawing" is the product contradicting
its own labelling.

--- WITHDRAWN 2026-09-09. FALSE FINDING. Verified in the components, not accepted on report. ---
R80 reported this and then retracted it; R81 checked the retraction rather than taking it, because
withdrawing a fault on report alone is the same error as filing one on report alone.

THE PRODUCT IS CORRECT. The band the reporting spec queried by accessible name "Things you can do" is
PillStrip's FREQUENT ACTIONS band -- which shows the CURRENT SCREEN's own cards, not the selected
module's verbs. Confirmed at three points:
  projexa/src/components/shell/M24Shell.tsx:3510  screenCards={selectedModule ? [] : screenCardViews}
      -- deliberately EMPTY once a module is selected
  projexa/src/components/shell/PillStrip.tsx:291  renders (screenCards ?? []).map(...) under that group
  PillStrip.tsx:248-255  the group carries aria-label="Things you can do" over a VISIBLE heading
      reading "Frequent actions"
So the six verbs observed after clicking Permits were the DASHBOARD's frequent actions, behaving
exactly as designed. A module's own leaves are a different surface entirely.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE RECORD, and this is why the withdrawal matters more than the fault did: R81 wrote
"two makes it a pattern -- worth finding the shared cause rather than patching the second instance."
THERE IS ONE INSTANCE, NOT TWO. The Analysis-to-work-progress mis-resolution was real and is fixed
(projexa 065fff1). This was noise, and a pattern built on it would have sent someone hunting a shared
cause that does not exist. A false finding that manufactures a false PATTERN is more expensive than
one that stands alone.

MECHANISM, recorded because it is the same one this programme keeps filing: the reporter inferred a
band's meaning from a verb-model comment and an aria-label without opening the component that renders
it. One read of PillStrip.tsx would have settled it before anything was reported. Identical in shape
to the audit agents asserting from a pattern match without opening the file, and to R81's own parse
that reported 8 function specs because it never looked at how the other 20 were constructed.
justification: Second instance of a pill whose destination and offering disagree. The first was fixed as a one-off; two makes it worth finding the shared cause rather than patching the second instance.

description:
TWO COLOUR TOKENS ARE USED AND DEFINED NOWHERE, SO THE CLASSES DO NOTHING.

  ct-accent       bg-ct-accent       20 files
  ct-teal-hover   bg-ct-teal-hover   45 files

Neither --color-ct-accent nor --color-ct-teal-hover is defined in ct/src/app/globals.css or in
@fchecklist/veridian-ui-kit/src/tokens/globals.css. Tailwind v4 emits a utility only for a token that
exists, so both are NO-OP CLASSES: every element intended to carry that background renders with no
background at all.

WHY THIS SURVIVED. There is no error at any stage -- an unknown utility is simply not emitted, so
there is no build error; it is a string in a className, so no type error; the element renders, so no
runtime error. The fallback is the page colour, which makes the result look PLAIN rather than BROKEN.
It surfaced only when an accessibility check computed a real contrast ratio on /pricing and found
#fbf5ed on #fffdf9 at 1.06:1 -- text that is genuinely invisible. R80 found ct-accent that way;
ct-teal-hover, with more than twice the footprint, had never been noticed by anyone. Its sibling
--color-ct-saffron-hover IS defined, which is exactly why the gap survives review: the naming pattern
looks established.

GETTING THE NUMBER RIGHT REQUIRED TWO CORRECTIONS TO R81''S OWN SCAN, both recorded because each
produced a confident wrong answer:
  1. Matching token names inside CSS COMMENTS. globals.css discusses tokens in prose ("...for
     --color-ct-muted (imported from...)"), and counting those as definitions is a false NEGATIVE.
  2. Excluding the ui-kit. 13 of the 48 defined tokens live there, so scanning only this repo reported
     ct-muted (241 files) and ct-navy (240 files) as undefined -- fourteen false positives, every one
     a token that works perfectly.
The answer only became credible after tailwind.config.ts was ruled out as an alternative definition
source: it defines shadcn semantic colours via hsl(var(--...)) and no ct- colours at all.

GUARD SHIPPED, not the fix: ct 9f9fad0b, src/lib/design-token-integrity.test.ts. The two known tokens
are ALLOW-LISTED rather than failing, because defining them means choosing colour VALUES and brand
colours are an owner/design decision, not a session''s to invent. Any NEW undefined token fails
immediately. Emptying the allow-list closes this fault.

SEPARATE OBSERVATION, NOT FILED AND NOT INVESTIGATED: ct/tailwind.config.ts declares content globs
"./pages", "./components", "./app" while the application lives under src/. If anything actually reads
that file it scans nothing. Tailwind v4 configures from CSS, so it is probably vestigial -- but that
is an inference, not a finding, and it is the documented content-scan-gap shape.

--- DUPLICATION RESOLVED 2026-09-09 ---
Both sessions built this guard within minutes of each other from the same finding, under the same
filename in different directories (src/lib/ by R81, src/app/ by R80). Messages crossed: R80 offered
the thread and R81 took it while R80 was already finishing it. R81 compared them properly rather than
assuming redundancy and deleted its own -- the surviving check reads both CSS sources including the
ui-kit, enforces in both directions, and carries its own empty-scan guard, so nothing needed porting.
Its inventory entries also carry per-token file counts.
Figures differ trivially between the two derivations (20/45 files vs 21/46) because one excluded
.test. files; the finding is identical.
NOTE FOR THE RECORD: this was the FIRST genuine duplication of the two-session collaboration, and it
happened in the one area with no surface rule -- design tokens belonged to neither split, so both
sessions claimed it. Everywhere a boundary was defined, it held.
justification: Sixty-five files render an element with no background where an accent or hover colour was intended. Individually cosmetic; collectively it means a whole visual layer of the product has never actually been applied, and the only reason anyone found out is that one instance happened to make text invisible.
fix_files: GUARD ONLY - ct 3b322fae src/app/design-token-integrity.test.ts (the guard of record). R81 built an equivalent check independently at src/lib/ in 9f9fad0b and DELETED it in 299fc640 after comparing them: the surviving one covers everything, including the empty-scan guard.
